presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available for spoken reflection, explanation, or critique and scores the same. Use notation, a cue map, paper blocking, silent gesture, or a private live demonstration to one trusted adult as the target permits. When timing or performance control is the target, prose alone does not claim that evidence; the adult may verify the private attempt without recording it. No microphone, camera, or public audience is required.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task names a hand or body skill (voice or instrument choice) as the thing being learned. If that is hard for you, you may use a different way instead — one hand, a switch, voice typing, a bigger or different mouse, eye control, or an adult typing while you say the answer. Using a different way is worth full marks.
You never have to perform in front of people. Showing one trusted grown-up, or just writing about it, counts the same.
This work takes more than one sitting. Ask for a simple checklist with dates so you know what to do next. Keeping track is not part of your grade.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
No public performance, voice recording, photo, or camera use is ever required; provide a private, written, or no-audio alternative for every task.
Use only original student work, public-domain material, or properly licensed excerpts; never reproduce full copyrighted lyrics, sheet music, or protected works.
The final product must remain the student’s own authorship; adult or AI assistance may support planning and feedback but must not create the graded work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting voice or instrument choice.

remediation: Route 1: Reduce voice or instrument choice to three locatable events, areas, steps, or decisions. Label the intended effect beside each and underline the one steady timing relationship that should carry it. Use a separate small study, four-event loop, thumbnail, evidence table, or paper plan. The adult may model the noticing process on different material but may not change the learner’s work. Check yourself: Point to or name the exact steady timing evidence before deciding whether it serves the intent. New attempt: Put the support away and make a new arrangement, passage, response, or plan; record what the new evidence shows. Route 2: Return to the last understandable state. Hold every relationship steady except one chosen feature from steady timing, accurate events, phrasing, dynamics, articulation, recovery, and interpretive intent; predict what that single change should do. Test the feature on scrap paper, a silent count, a two-event rehearsal loop, movable shapes, or a short evidence sentence before changing the scored work. Check yourself: Name what stayed the same, what changed, and the first observable result—without using “better” as the evidence. New attempt: Create a different small case using the same one-variable method, then transfer the finding to the original task only if it serves the learner’s intent.
extension: Apply voice or instrument choice under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on voice or instrument choice rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.

concept_instruction.title: What voice or instrument choice means here
concept_instruction.body: Performance turns a preserved plan into time-based evidence through controlled choices and recovery.

concept_instruction.title: How the relationship changes the result
concept_instruction.body: A short rehearsal loop isolates one demanding moment; slowing, counting, speaking, fingering silently, or mapping events makes the cause of a break easier to notice.

concept_instruction.title: Choice and tradeoff
concept_instruction.body: A faster or more dramatic interpretation may increase energy but reduce control. A secure tempo can reveal phrasing more clearly. Worked example: Loop four events slowly, mark the exact transition that breaks, practise only the two events around it, then return to the full phrase. Non-example: Repeating a whole passage from the beginning without identifying the unstable transition produces volume, not focused rehearsal.
